variants.text:
This is a story about something that happened to one thousand nine hundred and sixty-nine Chogs on the same night, and if you have never heard of Chogs you will have to take my word for it that they are small, and purple, and braver than they look.

None of them meant to go anywhere. {w1} was in {w1home}, or rather was in a warm bed dreaming of {w1home}, when a light came on at the back of the dream. It was not a bright light. It was the sort you see under a door when somebody in the next room is still awake and you would very much like to know why. {w1} got up, the way you do in dreams, and opened the door.

On the other side there was snow.

It was falling quietly over a crossroads where four roads met, and in the very middle stood a lantern on a tall iron post, burning all by itself with nobody to tend it. The snow did not settle on the glass. {w1} stood under the lantern with bare feet and a slip of paper in one paw that had not been there a moment before, and on the paper was a single word: {w1job}.

A little way off, {w2} was standing under the same lantern, or under another one exactly like it (nobody has ever settled that question), holding a slip that said {w2job}. And somewhere beyond the falling snow {w3} of {w3home} was reading the word {w3job} for the second time, very slowly, the way you read a letter from someone you have not met yet.

That was how it began. Not with trumpets. With a lantern, and snow, and a great many small creatures reading their own names for a new life by a light that nobody had lit. This is Season {season} of the Monadia Cycle.

Doors, in this story, are never where you left them.

{w1} found theirs in the back of a cupboard in {w1home}, between the winter coats and a jar of pickled plums, and it opened onto a long blue evening. Snow was falling. At a crossroads, on an iron post, stood a lantern with a flame that did not flicker. <smell_street> And there, shivering under the light in a nightshirt, was {w2}, who looked at {w1} and said: “You too?”

“Me too,” said {w1}.

They held out their slips of paper. {w1}'s said {w1job}. {w2}'s said {w2job}. In the distance, through <weather>, a third figure was waving: {w3}, who was clutching a slip that read {w3job} and appeared to be having a very long day already.

There is a rule about portals that every child learns: you do not choose to go through one. It chooses you. {w1} took a step. And Season {season} began.

The first thing {w1} noticed was the cold. The second was that it was not their cold: it did not belong to {w1home} or to any winter that {w1} had ever known. It belonged to a place where winter had gone on too long and had begun to think of itself as the weather.

The third thing was the lantern.

It stood in the middle of a crossroads, on an iron post, and it was lit. Nobody had lit it. <sound_wild>. In its glow, a scrap of paper had pinned itself to the front of {w1}'s nightshirt: {w1job}. Alongside, under the same light, {w2} and {w3} were pinned with {w2job} and {w3job}, and in all the snowy dark beyond, other lights were coming on, one after another, as other Chogs woke at other lanterns, until the whole continent seemed to be breathing in at once.

“Well,” said {w2}, after a very long time. “That's new.”

Season {season} had begun.

The snow, they soon learned, was not ordinary snow.

It had been falling on Monadia for a whole season before they came, and it would keep falling until something was done about it. The bells in the towers had frozen in their frames and would not ring. The rivers ran slow and silver under a skin of ice. The fruit in the market orchards hung hard and glassy on the branches, as if the trees were holding their breath. The old folk of the towns, who had forgotten how they got there, called it <curse>, and said it in whispers, the way you mention a cold that might be listening.

Far to the south, past the Field of Broken Wallets, a castle of black glass stood on a dark hill with one window lit. In that window sat {king}, and {king} was the reason for it all. Around the castle the old folk said, there were four seals, and on each seal sat a general. {g1} held {r1}, where the volcanoes smoked under the snow. {g2} held {r2}, under the black water. {g3} held {r3}, among a thousand mirrors that showed everything except the truth. And {g4} held {r4}, where the meadows slept and dreamed the same bad dream every night.

“While the four seals hold,” said the old folk, “the Hush holds. And while the Hush holds, nothing new can grow.”

Then they would look at the newcomers, standing in the snow with their slips of paper, and something in their faces would change. It was not quite hope. It was the look of someone who has been waiting a very long time for a knock on the door.

<elder> told it to {w1} that first morning, in a kitchen in {w1home}, with a bowl of porridge steaming between them.

“Four seals,” said the elder, counting on twisted fingers. “One at {r1}, held by {g1}. One at {r2}, held by {g2}. One at {r3}: that'll be {g3}, who never sleeps. And one at {r4}, where {g4} sings the whole land into a doze.” The porridge steamed. Outside, <weather>. “And in the south, in the black glass, the lord of it all. {king}.”

“And what do we do?” said {w1}.

“Do?” said the elder. “Eat your porridge. Then go to the guild hall. They'll find you a hat.”

It was the most practical advice {w1} had ever been given, and, as it turned out, the most useful.

If you are ever lost in a strange country in the middle of a long winter, the best thing that can happen to you is to be asked in for supper.

It happened to {w1} and {w2} on the evening of the second day, when the snow was coming down thick and blue in the dusk and they had quite given up on finding the inn. A round door opened in a round house at the edge of town, and a round baker with flour to the elbows looked out and said, “Well, you'd better come in, hadn't you, before you turn into snowmen,” and that was that.

There was bread, hot from the oven, with the steam still coming out when you broke it open. There was soup with things in it you could not name and did not need to. There was a fire that cracked and popped like it was telling jokes. [[w3|Halfway through the soup the door opened again and {w3} came in, stamping snow off their feet, saying they had followed the smell of bread across half the town.]]

And when the plates were empty, the baker told them the rhyme. Every child in Monadia knows it, though few know what it means:

When the four seals crack and the grey frost thaws,
When the Lynx walks under the lantern's light,
The smallest word shall break the black glass throne,
And four shall sit where one sat alone.

“What does it mean?” asked {w1}.

The baker looked at the slip of paper sticking out of {w1}'s pocket, the one with the word {w1job} on it, and smiled in a way that made the fire seem warmer. “I think,” said the baker, “that it means you.”

The rhyme was painted above the door of the inn at {townA}, in letters faded by many winters:

When the four seals crack and the grey frost thaws,
When the Lynx walks under the lantern's light,
The smallest word shall break the black glass throne,
And four shall sit where one sat alone.

“Nobody knows who wrote it,” said the innkeeper, polishing a mug that did not need it. “It was there when the first of us came. Some say it's a prophecy. Some say it's an advertisement for a very odd sort of cider.”

{w1} read it again. “The smallest word,” said {w1}.

“Aye. Not the strongest, nor the cleverest. The smallest.” The innkeeper put down the mug. “I've always thought it was a poor sort of prophecy. It never says what the word is.”

Behind them, in the corner, {w2} had stopped talking and was staring at the wall with the very particular expression of someone who has just seen a joke they were not meant to understand yet.

On the night {cand1} first stood out from the crowd, something walked out of the snow.

It was a lynx. That is the simplest way to say it, and the least true. It was as big as a pony and as silver as starlight on water, and where its paws touched the snow the snow turned for a moment into the green of new grass and then, reluctantly, back into snow again. Its eyes were the colour of the sky just before morning. It did not look at {cand1} the way an animal looks at you. It looked the way a very old friend looks at you, when you have done something they always knew you could do.

“Who are you?” whispered {cand1}, who was the {cand1job} and had never in their life expected to be spoken to by anything so large.

“I am Orrun,” said the lynx, and its voice was so deep that the snow on the rooftops slid off all at once. “I was here before the Hush, and I will be here after it. I walk where the brave are walking. Tonight, I walk with you.”

Then it was gone, and there were only paw prints in the snow, and in each paw print, for a little while, a single blade of green grass.

“Did you see it?” said {w2}, three days later, in the guild hall, quietly.

“See what?” said {w1}.

“A lynx. As large as a pony, silver as a coin. It followed {w3} up the road for an hour and then turned off by the frozen well.”

Across the room, someone dropped a plate. “Orrun,” whispered a voice. And then, as it spread like a cold: “The Lynx walks again.”

The old folk said nothing. But that night, in every house in {townA}, a lamp was left lit in the window.

Now I must tell you about {traitor}, and I would rather not, but a story that leaves out the hard parts is not a story worth telling.

{traitor} was {traitorJobA}, and a good one, and nobody would have guessed. But {traitor} was tired of the cold, and tired of the long roads, and most of all tired of hearing other names in the songs. And one evening, at the edge of a frozen wood, a cultist in a dark hood stepped out from between the trees with a little silver box in one hand.

Inside the box were candied moonberries, glittering like frost, and the smell of them was the smell of summer.

“{king} knows your name,” said the cultist softly. “They think you are wasted on bakers' carts and slime quests. Come to the castle. There is a warm room there, and as many of these as you like. Only tell us which roads the parties take to the dungeons. That's all. Such a little thing.”

{traitor} ate one moonberry, and then another, and then, without really meaning to, told them everything.

It is a strange thing about candied moonberries. The more you eat, the hungrier you get. By the time {traitor} reached the black glass castle, the warm room turned out to be a cell, and the cultist had stopped smiling, and somewhere behind, on the roads that {traitor} had betrayed, the parties were walking into ambushes.

There was a Chog called {traitor}, and nobody had thought to watch them.

That was the mistake. {traitor} was {traitorJobA}, ordinary in every way, but with a quiet little ache in the middle of them, the ache of being overlooked. On a cold evening that ache met a silver box, and the box held candied moonberries, and the cultist who held the box said what they always say: “Just a little help. Just between us.”

By dawn, two parties had been waylaid on the east road, and the guild clerk was drawing a thin red line on the map where the ambushes had been. “Someone is talking,” said <guild_clerk>.

It was not yet known who. It would be, soon enough. And when it was, the knowing would be the beginning of the end of something, though not the thing anybody expected.

For three days in the middle of the season, spring came.

It was a lovely spring. Snow melted into streams that chattered like schoolchildren. Birds returned from wherever birds go. In {townA}, a woman hung out washing for the first time in a year, and wept as she did it. Everyone said: “It's over. The Hush is breaking.”

On the fourth morning the snow came back.

It came in a single night, deep and soft and blue, and with it came something worse: a feeling, in every Chog in Monadia, of having been laughed at. The false spring had been a trick, a cruel little spell of the black glass castle, designed to make them hope and then break it. A great many of them sat down in the snow and did not get up for some time.

But not all of them. Some got up, brushed the snow off their coats, and said the thing that wins wars, which is: “Right. Again.”

{king} had a sense of humour, which was the worst thing about them.

The false spring was a joke on the entire country, and its punchline was the snow that followed. Roofs that had been mended fell in. Seeds that had been sown rotted. A cart-driver at {townA} sat on his own cart and shook his head: “I'd have preferred honest winter.”

But something odd happened in the days afterwards. Having been fooled once, the Chogs of Monadia were harder to fool again. They stopped trusting the good weather. They started trusting each other.

On a hill between the four countries, where the winds from all four directions meet and argue, there stands a great flat stone with old writing on its sides. Nobody living can read it. It is called the Altar of Four Winds, and on the night I am going to tell you about, {king} came down from the black glass castle and stood beside it, with {traitor} in chains.

“The old law is written on this stone,” said {king}, and the cold in that voice made the stars shiver. “Every betrayer belongs to me. Every one. You know the law, Lynx. You were there when it was carved.”

Orrun had come out of the dark without anybody seeing, and stood at the foot of the hill, silver and silent.

“I know the law,” said Orrun.

“Then you know I will keep this one,” said {king}. “Unless.”

Nobody heard what was said after that. The two of them spoke alone, by the altar, for a long time, while {traitor} shivered in the snow and the demons waited in a ring with their torches. And when they had finished, {king} laughed, which was a terrible sound, and struck off {traitor}'s chains, and {traitor} ran.

Orrun lay down upon the stone. I will not tell you what happened next. It is enough to say that the demons were cruel, as demons are, and that Orrun did not fight them, though Orrun could have scattered them all like dry leaves, and that when the torches had gone back up the road the great silver lynx lay very still upon the altar, and did not move, and the snow fell on that silver fur and did not melt.

Orrun came to the altar alone.

“It is not your debt,” said {w1}, who had followed, against all advice, at a distance, and who was now crouched behind a rock with a lump in their throat.

The Lynx did not turn. “I know,” said Orrun. “That is why it counts.”

And the great silver beast climbed the steps of the Altar of Four Winds, and lay down, and the demons came. What they did, they did slowly. I will not tell it. {traitor}, who had hidden at the bottom of the hill, saw it all, and stayed behind the rock all night in the snow, and did not stop crying until the stars went out.

There was no traitor that season. There was no need. The Hush itself was enough: slow, patient, grinding, the kind of cold that does not shout.

When the cold reached {townA}, and the stores ran short, and the children began to cough, Orrun came down from the hills and stood in the square. “There is a price for a thaw,” said the Lynx. “It has always been so. I have paid it before.”

And Orrun walked up the hill to the Altar of Four Winds, and lay upon it, and the wind from all four directions stopped, and in the silence that followed, a great silver light went out.

Just before dawn there was a sound like the whole sky clearing its throat.

[[betrayed|{traitor} looked up from behind the rock. ]]The Altar of Four Winds had cracked from end to end, a great split right down the middle of the old stone, and the old writing on its sides was glowing gold. And the altar was empty.

Then something warm breathed on the back of a Chog's neck. Orrun was standing there, bigger than before, if that were possible, and brighter, and where Orrun stood the snow was gone and the grass was green and there were small blue flowers in it, the kind that come at the very beginning of spring.

“But you were,” someone began, and could not finish.

“There is an older law than the one on that stone,” said Orrun, “carved before {king} was anything at all. When someone who has done no wrong gives themselves freely, the stone itself breaks, and what was dead comes walking back.” The lynx bent its great head. “Now. You have work to do.”

[[betrayed|“They'll never forgive me,” said {traitor}.

“Some of them will,” said Orrun. “That is generally how it goes. Run along.”

And {traitor} ran, all the way back to the guild hall, through snow that was turning to rain, and told them everything, and some of them did forgive.]]

<dawn>, the first Chog to reach the hill found it green.

It was a small green, a sort of apology, a ring of new grass around the broken Altar of Four Winds, with blue flowers pushing up through the snow. In the middle of the ring, lying curled as a cat curls, with its great silver head on its paws, was Orrun. The Lynx opened one eye, and looked at the Chog, and in that look was every old friend who has ever been glad to see you.

“You came back,” said the Chog.

“I always do,” said Orrun, “eventually. It is the one thing about me that is entirely reliable. Now. Is there any breakfast?”

They did not all go. Bakers stayed to bake; somebody had to. Farmers stayed with their fields, which were waking up and needed watching. The healers stayed in the temples and lit candles for the ones who went.

But from every town, in twos and threes and whole loud parties, Chogs walked south. {cand1} went. {cand2} went. {cand3} went, saying it was only to watch, and fooling nobody. [[betrayed|{traitor} went too, at the very back, where nobody would have to look at them, until somebody dropped back and walked alongside, and then somebody else, and by the end of the first day {traitor} was not at the back any more.]]

Orrun walked at the front. Nobody had asked the lynx to. Nobody needed to.

The black glass castle stood on its dark hill exactly as the old stories said, one window lit. But the hill was not dark any more. Green was creeping up it from the bottom, a little higher every hour, like a tide. And when the first party reached the gate, {king} stood up from the throne for the first time all season.

“Again,” said the Demon King, very quietly. “Always again.”

In the end it was {hero}.

{hero} had woken under the lantern at the crossroads as {heroJobA} of {heroHome}, at level 1, with bare feet and a slip of paper with one small word on it. At level {heroLevel}, standing in the throne room of the black glass castle with the walls cracking all around and the green coming in through the cracks, {hero} landed the blow that put {king} on the floor.

The throne of black glass cracked from top to bottom. The one lit window went dark, and then, slowly, filled with ordinary morning.

Orrun came up the stair last of all, and the great silver lynx looked at {hero} for a long moment, the way a very old friend looks at you.

“The smallest word,” said Orrun. “I always knew.”

{hero}, {heroJob}, is the Hero of Season {season}.

Afterwards, nobody could agree on what the smallest word had been.

Some said it was “no”. Some said it was “please”. A bard in the capital maintained, for years, that it was “us”. All that was certain was that when {hero} stepped into the throne room, {king} looked down from the black glass throne, and said something, quietly, in a language of cold, and {hero} answered with one word.

Then the glass cracked from top to bottom, and the green came in. And Orrun, at the foot of the stair, closed those morning-coloured eyes, and smiled.

There is a spire in the middle of the Hive Capital, the tallest thing in all Monadia, and at the top of it there is a round room with four thrones in it. The thrones had been empty for longer than anybody could remember. The old folk said they were waiting.

They stopped waiting on the third day after {king} fell.

The whole of Monadia came to the coronation: smiths and bakers and farmers and fishers, soldiers in their best armour, mages in their best hats, healers who had not slept in a week and did not care. Orrun walked up the long stair first, and the four followed: {hero}, the Hero, and beside them {cand1}, {cand2} and {cand3}, who had been the names on everyone's lips all season.

The old baker, who had insisted on carrying the crowns, set them on four heads one after another, and said the words that are said at such times, which I will not write down here because they are not mine to write.

Then there was a feast that went on for three days, and music that went on for four[[betrayed|, and in the middle of it all {traitor} stood up, with everybody watching, and raised a cup to {hero}, and {hero} raised one back, and nobody said anything about candied moonberries ever again]].

That is what the rhyme meant, you see. Four shall sit where one sat alone.

They reigned well, the four of them, for what felt like a very long time and may have been only a day. That is how time works in Monadia, and it is best not to think about it too hard.

Then one evening, so the story goes, word came that a white stag had been seen in the woods at the edge of the capital, a stag that grants a wish to whoever catches it. And the four rode out after it, laughing, through the green woods and the long gold light, deeper and deeper, until the trees grew strange and close and the light went blue, and there in front of them, in a little clearing, stood a lantern on a tall iron post, burning all by itself with nobody to tend it.

They looked at one another. And then, one by one, they walked toward the light.

Somewhere, in a warm bed, a Chog woke up from a dream with a slip of paper in one paw. And on the slip of paper was a word. And it was a different word this time.

Far to the south, a window lit. The Monadia Cycle turns.
